title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Both Parts
quickIdea: Part 1 says differentiating an integral with a variable upper limit gives the integrand back; part 2 says a definite integral is any antiderivative evaluated at the two ends.
remember: Part 1: if f is continuous and F(x) is the integral of f from a to x, then F'(x) = f(x). The integral with a variable limit is a function; its slope at x is the height of the curve there.

With a function in the limit the chain rule applies: d/dx of the integral from a to g(x) of f equals f(g(x)) times g'(x). With a constant lower limit and a variable upper limit, no minus sign appears; the minus sign appears only when the variable sits in the lower limit.
Part 2: if F is any antiderivative of f on [a, b], the integral from a to b of f is F(b) - F(a). This is what turns the whole of this topic into table lookup plus technique.
The theorem needs f continuous on the interval; a jump in f makes the integral-with-variable-limit fail to be differentiable at that point.
Equations with an integral in them are solved by part 2: integrate, then solve the resulting algebraic equation for the unknown limit.

example.prompt: Differentiate the integral of e^t from 0 to x^2 with respect to x, and evaluate the integral of t from 1 to x, then solve that integral equal to 1/4 for x greater than 1.
example.work: Part 1 with the chain rule: the derivative is e^(x^2) times 2x. For the second, an antiderivative of t is t^2/2, so the integral from 1 to x is (x^2 - 1)/2. Setting (x^2 - 1)/2 = 1/4 gives x^2 - 1 = 1/2, so x^2 = 3/2 and x = sqrt(3/2) = 1.2247.
example.answer: 2x e^(x^2); and x = sqrt(3/2) solves the second part.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.2 is exactly the second half of this card: the equation integral from 1 to x of t ln t dt = 1/4, solved by applying part 2 and then solving for x, giving sqrt(e). The variable-limit form of part 1 is the standard distractor in statement questions, where an option offers f(x) instead of f(g(x)) g'(x).

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.2: the value of x greater than 1 satisfying the integral from 1 to x of t ln t dt = 1/4 is (A) sqrt(e) (B) e (C) e^2 (D) e - 1.
variations.why: By parts gives the antiderivative t^2 ln t / 2 - t^2/4, so the integral from 1 to x is x^2 ln x / 2 - x^2/4 + 1/4. Setting it equal to 1/4 leaves x^2(2 ln x - 1)/4 = 0, and since x is positive and greater than 1 the bracket must vanish: ln x = 1/2.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Find d/dx of the integral from x to 5 of sin(t^2) dt.
variations.why: Reversing the limits introduces a minus sign: the integral from x to 5 is minus the integral from 5 to x, whose derivative is sin(x^2) by part 1. This is the one place a sign is easy to lose, and it is why the card states the lower-limit case separately.

trap.what: Applying part 1 to a variable upper limit that is a function of x without the chain-rule factor, or forgetting the minus sign when x sits in the lower limit.
trap.why: The theorem is stated for the upper limit being x itself; any other function g(x) needs f(g(x)) g'(x). And swapping the limits is a sign change, not a rewrite.
trap.counterexample: d/dx of the integral from 0 to x^2 of e^t dt is 2x e^(x^2), not e^(x^2): at x = 2 the correct value is 4 e^4 = 218.39 while e^(x^2) = 54.60. At x = 0 the careless answer gives 1 while the true slope is 0.

check.question: What is d/dx of the integral from 0 to x^2 of e^t dt at x = 0?
check.explanation: The derivative is 2x e^(x^2), which vanishes at x = 0. This is a useful sanity check: the integral from 0 to x^2 has a minimum at x = 0, so its slope there must be zero.
